steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on invariant checking for SMT-based transition systems with quantifiers. Motivate why quantifiers and theories are needed, say where prior work falls short, describe our two algorithms and the evaluation, and give the structure of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Model checking and the need for quantifiers (parameterized systems)
2. Limitations of previous work
3. Problem statement and formalism (array-based transition systems)
4. First algorithm: UPDR + implicit abstraction
5. Second algorithm: finite-cardinality instance, generalization, validity check
6. Evaluation, relation to earlier papers, paper structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- model checking: automatically prove/disprove property of system
- symbolic algorithms with quantifier-free SAT/SMT: big progress recently
- many areas need first-order quantifiers in system description and property
- parameterized systems: finite but unbounded number of components; e.g. communication protocols (leader election), feature systems, control algorithms (railways interlocking logic)
- challenge: correctness for all configurations / parameter instantiations

2. Prior work
- theories + quantifiers combined: far from trivial
- SMT-based parameterized verification: strong syntactic restrictions
- other quantified model checking approaches: less restrictive, no theories

3. Problem
- invariant properties of symbolic transition systems in quantified first-order logic modulo theories
- state variables = functions from finite but unbounded domains
- formalism: array-based transition systems (expanding earlier notion)
- two fully automated approaches

4. Algorithm 1
- based on UPDR: extension of IC3/PDR synthesizing universally quantified invariants
- combined with implicit abstraction for general SMT theories
- implicit abstraction previously used to extend IC3 to quantifier-free infinite-state systems; we modify it for quantified systems
- lift several properties of original algorithm
- drawback: heavy reliance on quantified queries to external solver, expensive

5. Algorithm 2
- restrict cardinality of uninterpreted sort to fixed number -> quantifier-free system, existing model checkers
- result: counterexample (unsafe) or quantifier-free inductive invariant
- generalize invariant to quantified candidate; check validity via abstraction or quantified SMT
- valid -> safe; else e.g. increase cardinality and iterate
- option 1: extension of Parameter Abstraction -> quantifier-free system + property
- option 2: off-the-shelf SMT solver with quantifiers (e.g. Z3); black box may diverge
- resource-bounded instantiation for more controlled quantified queries

6. Evaluation / structure
- both implemented, large benchmark set from different sources; theories, quantifier alternations, or both
- very general, compare well with other tools; first to handle such variety uniformly
- second algorithm combines earlier algorithms, unified description, larger benchmarks
- sections: 2 background; 3 formalism + problem; 4 first algorithm; 5 second; 6 related work; 7 experiments; 8 conclusions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Model checking algorithms are made to prove or disprove automatically that a property holds in a given system. Symbolic algorithms in particular, which are based on efficient quantifier-free SAT and SMT reasoning, have made a lot of progress in recent years. But many verification areas need first-order quantifiers, both in the symbolic description of the system and in the property to prove. One example is the verification of parameterized systems, which consist of a finite but unbounded number of components. Examples of such systems are communication protocols (e.g. leader election), feature systems, or control algorithms in different application domains (e.g. railways interlocking logic). The main challenge is to prove that the system is correct for all the possible configurations that correspond to instantiations of the parameters.

Unfortunately dealing with transition systems with theories and quantifiers combined is far from trivial. Previous works that verify parameterized systems with SMT-based techniques impose strong syntactic restrictions on which formulae are supported. Other existing approaches for model checking systems with quantifiers are less restrictive, but they do not support theories.

In this paper we discuss the problem of model checking invariant properties of symbolic transition systems that are expressed in quantified first-order logic modulo theories, where the state variables are functions from finite but unbounded domains.

We first define our formalism using the notion of array-based transition systems (which expands an earlier notion), which is suited for describing systems like the ones above. Then we propose two fully automated approaches to solve the invariant problem of array-based systems.

The first algorithm is based on UPDR, which is an extension of the IC3/PDR algorithm that synthesizes universally quantified invariants. Our procedure combines UPDR with implicit abstraction so that it can deal with general SMT theories. Implicit abstraction was used in earlier work to extend IC3 to quantifier-free infinite-state systems. In this paper we show how to modify that technique so that it handles quantified systems too. We also lift several properties of the original algorithm to our setting. But the resulting algorithm relies heavily on quantified queries to an external solver, and in practice this is still an expensive subroutine.

- Algorithm 2: fix cardinality of uninterpreted sort -> quantifier-free system, existing techniques -> counterexample (unsafe) or quantifier-free inductive invariant
- generalize to quantified candidate invariant, check validity (abstraction or quantified SMT); valid -> safe, else e.g. increase cardinality and iterate
- option 1: extension of Parameter Abstraction (quantifier-free system + property)
- option 2: off-the-shelf solver like Z3, but black box may diverge -> resource-bounded instantiation

- evaluation: both implemented, large benchmark set (theories, quantifier alternations, or both); general, compare well; first uniform approach for such variety
- second algorithm = combination of earlier algorithms, unified, more benchmarks
- structure: Sections 2-8

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Model checking algorithms are made to prove or disprove automatically that a property holds in a given system. Symbolic algorithms in particular, which are based on efficient quantifier-free SAT and SMT reasoning, have made a lot of progress in recent years. But many verification areas need first-order quantifiers, both in the symbolic description of the system and in the property to prove. One example is the verification of parameterized systems, which consist of a finite but unbounded number of components. Examples of such systems are communication protocols (e.g. leader election), feature systems, or control algorithms in different application domains (e.g. railways interlocking logic). The main challenge is to prove that the system is correct for all the possible configurations that correspond to instantiations of the parameters.

Unfortunately dealing with transition systems with theories and quantifiers combined is far from trivial. Previous works that verify parameterized systems with SMT-based techniques impose strong syntactic restrictions on which formulae are supported. Other existing approaches for model checking systems with quantifiers are less restrictive, but they do not support theories.

In this paper we discuss the problem of model checking invariant properties of symbolic transition systems that are expressed in quantified first-order logic modulo theories, where the state variables are functions from finite but unbounded domains.

We first define our formalism using the notion of array-based transition systems (which expands an earlier notion), which is suited for describing systems like the ones above. Then we propose two fully automated approaches to solve the invariant problem of array-based systems.

The first algorithm is based on UPDR, which is an extension of the IC3/PDR algorithm that synthesizes universally quantified invariants. Our procedure combines UPDR with implicit abstraction so that it can deal with general SMT theories. Implicit abstraction was used in earlier work to extend IC3 to quantifier-free infinite-state systems. In this paper we show how to modify that technique so that it handles quantified systems too. We also lift several properties of the original algorithm to our setting. But the resulting algorithm relies heavily on quantified queries to an external solver, and in practice this is still an expensive subroutine.

The second algorithm is a simple but general procedure based on two key ingredients that interact. First we restrict the cardinality of the uninterpreted sort to a fixed natural number. This gives a quantifier-free system which can be model-checked with existing techniques. When it terminates we either get a counterexample, and then the system is unsafe, or a proof of the property in the form of a quantifier-free inductive invariant. Second, the invariant is generalized to a quantified candidate invariant for the original system, and we check its validity with either a form of abstraction or quantified SMT reasoning. If the candidate invariant is valid, the system is safe. If not, more reasoning is needed, e.g. increasing the cardinality of the domain and iterating the first step. The first option for checking that a candidate invariant holds is based on extending the works on Parameter Abstraction to our formalism. This technique computes a quantifier-free system and a quantifier-free property, and if the property holds, the original property is an invariant of the system. The second option is to use any off-the-shelf solver that supports SMT and quantifiers (e.g. Z3) for the validity checks. But checking the validity of quantified formulae with a black-box approach may make the procedure diverge in practice. So we also propose a more careful approach to instantiation that is resource-bounded, which can be used to discharge quantified queries in a more controlled way.

We implemented both algorithms and evaluated them experimentally on a large set of benchmarks, which come from different sources and use theories, quantifier alternations, or both. The experiments show that the algorithms are very general and that they compare well with other tools in each category. As far as we know, our algorithms are the first that can approach such a large variety of systems in a uniform way.

Note that the second algorithm of this paper is a combination of two earlier algorithms, described in a unified way and evaluated experimentally on a larger set of benchmarks.

The structure of the paper is as follows. Section 2 gives some background. Section 3 introduces our formalism and states the problem of this work. Section 4 describes the first algorithm and Section 5 the second one. Section 6 discusses related work, and Section 7 has the experimental evaluation of both algorithms and the comparison with other tools. Section 8 draws conclusions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Model checking algorithms are designed to automatically prove or disprove that a given property holds in a system. In particular, symbolic algorithms based on efficient quantifier-free SAT and SMT reasoning have seen significant progress in the last few years. However, many verification areas need first-order quantifiers, both in the symbolic description of the system and in the property to prove. This is the case, for example, for the verification of parameterized systems, which consist of a finite but unbounded number of components. Examples include communication protocols (e.g. leader election), feature systems, or control algorithms in various application domains (e.g. railways interlocking logic). The key challenge is to prove the correctness of the system for all possible configurations corresponding to instantiations of the parameters.

Unfortunately, the combined case of transition systems with theories and quantifiers is far from trivial to deal with. Previous works on the verification of parameterized systems with SMT-based techniques, such as [1,2], impose strong syntactic restrictions on the supported formulae. Other approaches for model checking systems with quantifiers, such as [3,4,5], are less restrictive, but do not support theories.

In this paper, we discuss the problem of model checking invariant properties of symbolic transition systems expressed in quantified first-order logic modulo theories, with state variables that are functions from finite but unbounded domains.

We start by defining our formalism using the notion of array-based transition systems (expanding the notion from [6]), which is suited to describing systems as above. We then propose two fully automated approaches for solving the invariant problem of array-based systems.

The first algorithm is based on UPDR [4], an extension of the IC3/PDR algorithm that synthesizes universally quantified invariants. Our procedure combines UPDR with implicit abstraction [7] to deal with general SMT theories. Implicit abstraction was used in [8] to extend IC3 to quantifier-free infinite-state systems; in this paper, we show how to modify that technique to handle quantified systems as well, and we lift several properties of the original algorithm to our setting. However, the resulting algorithm relies heavily on quantified queries to an external solver, which in practice is still an expensive subroutine.

The second algorithm is a simple yet general procedure based on the interaction of two key ingredients. First, we restrict the cardinality of the uninterpreted sort to a fixed natural number. This yields a quantifier-free system that can be model-checked with existing techniques: upon termination, we get either a counterexample, in which case the system is unsafe, or a proof of the property in the form of a quantifier-free inductive invariant. Second, the invariant is generalized to a quantified candidate invariant for the original system, whose validity is checked using either a form of abstraction or quantified SMT reasoning. If the candidate invariant is valid, the system is safe. Otherwise, further reasoning is required, e.g. increasing the cardinality of the domain and iterating the first step. The first option for checking that a candidate invariant holds is based on extending the works on Parameter Abstraction of [9,10] to our formalism. This technique computes a quantifier-free system and a quantifier-free property which, if it holds, ensures that the original property is an invariant of the system. As a second option, we could instead use any off-the-shelf solver supporting SMT and quantifiers (e.g. Z3 [11]) to discharge the validity checks. However, a black-box approach to checking the validity of quantified formulae may cause the procedure to diverge in practice. We therefore also propose a more careful, resource-bounded approach to instantiation, which can be used to discharge quantified queries in a more controlled way.

Both algorithms have been implemented and experimentally evaluated over a large benchmark set obtained from different sources, which makes use of theories, quantifier alternations, or both. The experimental evaluation shows that the algorithms are very general and compare well with other tools in each category. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithms are the first able to approach such a large variety of systems in a uniform way.

We remark that the second algorithm of this paper combines the algorithms given in [12,13], describing them in a unified manner and evaluating them over a larger set of benchmarks.

The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 presents some background. In Section 3, we introduce our formalism and state the problem addressed in this work. Section 4 illustrates the first algorithm, and Section 5 describes the second one. We discuss related work in Section 6 and conduct the experimental evaluation of both algorithms, including a comparison with other tools, in Section 7. Finally, Section 8 draws conclusions.
